video.title: He Found a Grant That Feels Like a Cheat Code ($2.4M/Year)

summary: Hector describes building trade schools that sell online vocational courses, with state grants reimbursing tuition for eligible students. His main example is a forklift technician school connected to an existing repair business, where online lessons are paired with optional hands-on training and job leads. He also explains how he improved school sales systems, consulted for other schools, and helped clients sell training to employers, nonprofits, and other groups. The model depends on local licensing and funding rules, and the transcript mixes Hector’s operating claims with a sponsor read and a few unclear Whisper-transcribed figures.

speakers.description: Trade-school operator and consultant; surname not stated.

ideas.name: Grant-funded online forklift technician trade school

pricing.model: Course tuition, potentially reimbursed through a state grant.

ideas.delivery: The core curriculum is online and students take a computer-based test. Hands-on practice is optional for this course. In the connected forklift repair business, graduates can ride with technicians after about four weeks before being put on their own. Hector says he handles support, streamlining, automation, and CRM work while operating partners supply trade expertise.
unit_economics_claims: Hector reported $2.4 million in revenue in the first calendar year for his first school.
He reported $1.4 million in the second year, with a two-person operation.
He described roughly 70% margins for those years and the host characterized a course's tuition and content cost as nearly 90% margins.
The forklift course was quoted at $7,500, with $500 for the course and a claimed $7,000 margin.
The host described grants of $5,000 to $15,000 per student.
Hector said graduates typically had two or three interviews before receiving a job offer.
ideas.startup_cost: Hector estimated $15,000 to $30,000 for a new school, including state costs and operating capital. He said some states want two or three months of reserves. The forklift school was added to an existing repair business, so its separate startup cost was not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Hector said to start selling while the licensing process is underway in some states, but warned that requirements differ by state.

acquisition.how: Paid ads, referral requests, and online lead handling can be automated, but the transcript includes phone sales. In the UK, software should avoid unsolicited marketing to individuals and sole traders without consent; cold calls need TPS/CTPS screening.

onboarding.how: Online registration and course access could be automated, but grant eligibility, licensing, and student records require checks.

delivery.how: Online lessons and tests can run automatically. Optional hands-on training, job support, and technician ride-alongs require people.

billing.how: Online payment and grant invoicing could be handled by software after human review of eligibility and state reimbursement rules.

support.how: Course questions and reminders can be handled partly with automation, but the guest describes interacting with students and supporting job placement.

uk_applicability.notes: Online vocational training and employer demand can translate to the UK, but the state grant and licensing process described is US-specific. UK funding, accreditation, and qualification requirements would need to be established separately.

risks: Grant amounts, caps, licensing, and reserve requirements vary by state.
The guest says some states allow course sales without a school licence, but that does not establish that every course or sales route is lawful.
A computer-based test may verify curriculum knowledge without proving practical repair skill.
Hiring support and optional hands-on work reduce the degree to which delivery is fully remote.
The guest's early school spent heavily on a building, staff, furniture, and books that students did not use.

warnings.warning: Licensing, grant eligibility, reimbursement caps, and reserve requirements vary by state. Hector repeatedly advises checking the rules for the state or region.
The guest describes selling courses before being licensed as something the Arizona client did 'not by the book'; he says the client later became licensed.
The host's initial school spent on a building, staff, furniture, and books before learning that most students wanted online courses and did not attend in person.
A computer test may show that a student learned the curriculum without proving that they can perform the trade in practice.
The guest advises staying focused on one or two courses initially and says he would not offer more than three.
Some students may complete a course without following through into a job; the guest says it happens, though not as often as expected.
The host's Busy/Biz.com endorsement is a sponsor read and should be treated as promotional rather than independent evaluation.
The transcript says the Utah prison-training operator makes about '$30 in a month'; the unit or scale may be misheard and cannot be clarified from this transcript.
